clue.text: Respectable Windsor woman sees smart pig discomfited

indicators.note: discomfited means upset or thrown into disorder, so the three words before it are jumbled

explanation.surface: A respectable lady of Windsor is upset at the sight of a clever pig.
explanation.walkthrough: 'discomfited' shuffles SEES, SMART and PIG together. The sixth word of the clue is fodder too, not just a verb in the scene.
explanation.definitionFit: In Shakespeare's comedy The Merry Wives of Windsor, the virtuous wife who fools Falstaff is Mistress Page.

clue.text: Grace Aguilar's courtier Ferdinand sees Spain cocooned in ethics

indicators.note: cocooned in means wrapped inside, so the country's letter sits within the word for ethics

parts.note: ethics are morals, principles of conduct
E is the international vehicle code for Spain (España)

explanation.surface: A Spanish courtier in a Victorian novel is shown wrapped in moral principles.
explanation.walkthrough: Grace Aguilar's novel The Vale of Cedars features the courtier Ferdinand Morales; the solver needs the surname only.
explanation.definitionFit: Ferdinand Morales is a character at the Spanish court in Aguilar's historical novel The Vale of Cedars.

clue.text: She crewed with Charlie Allnut in Africa

definitions.text: She crewed with Charlie Allnut in Africa

parts.words: She crewed with Charlie Allnut in Africa
parts.note: points to the missionary's sister who sails downriver with Allnut in C.S. Forester's The African Queen

explanation.definitionFit: Rose, the spinster heroine of Forester's novel, travels with boatman Charlie Allnut; her surname is the entry.

clue.text: Unwilling, like E.R. Braithwaite's neighbours

definitions.meaning: unwilling means not wanting to do something
E.R. Braithwaite, author of To Sir, With Love, also wrote a book titled with this adjective before Neighbours

explanation.definitionFit: Unwilling is a plain synonym, and Braithwaite's 1972 book on race in Britain is titled with the same adjective.

clue.text: What's become of Waring Since he gave us all the (? Browning)

definitions.text: What's become of Waring Since he gave us all the (? Browning)

parts.words: What's become of Waring Since he gave us all the (? Browning)
parts.note: asks for the missing last word of the opening of Robert Browning's poem Waring

explanation.definitionFit: Browning's lines run 'What's become of Waring / Since he gave us all the' and end with the word meaning an escape.

clue.text: Tie chaps in a knot with style imitation

indicators.note: tied in a knot means twisted up, so the letters of the two words before it are tangled together

explanation.surface: Some men are tying their neckties into knots in imitation of a fashionable style.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a knot' shuffles TIE and CHAPS together; 'with' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A work written or painted in imitation of another's style is called by this French-derived word.

clue.text: Some dish Galahad was pursuing

parts.note: describes the sacred vessel of Arthurian legend, sought by the knight Galahad, as a mere dish

explanation.definitionFit: In Arthurian legend the holy vessel, sometimes pictured as a dish or platter, is the object of Galahad's quest.

clue.text: Conspirator lit up in undisciplined ship

indicators.note: in places the turned word inside the name of the ship

parts.note: the USS Caine is the ship whose crew mutinies in Herman Wouk's The Caine Mutiny

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from the bottom, backwards

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A plotter lights a fuse aboard a ship whose crew has broken discipline.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns LIT into TIL, and 'in' puts that inside CAINE. The undisciplined ship is the one from The Caine Mutiny.
explanation.definitionFit: Catiline led the conspiracy against the Roman Republic that Cicero exposed in 63 BC.

clue.text: Two such in Le Carré book, possibly allowed by one 12 at

definitions.text: Two such in Le Carré book
definitions.meaning: John le Carré's novel is titled with this word twice, joined by an ampersand
in cricket, someone fielding (the answer to 12) at a position may concede a run of one

explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference 12 gives FIELDING; a fielder who lets the ball past may allow the batsmen one run. Cricket's single is one run.
explanation.definitionFit: Le Carré's 1999 novel is Single & Single, and in cricket a one-run score is the same word.

clue.text: Ruler's accessories may accrue to author

definitions.meaning: the members of a monarch's family and entourage, persons of royal rank
payments made to a writer for each copy of a book sold

explanation.definitionFit: The word means both royal persons around a sovereign and the percentage payments a writer earns from sales.

clue.text: Instrument makers from Birmingham (at Italian rates)

indicators.note: from tells the solver to take the letters straight out of the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: Violins from a Birmingham workshop are being sold at Italian prices.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' takes the letters out of 'BirminghAM AT Italian'. 'rates' only completes the picture.
explanation.definitionFit: The family of Cremona craftsmen, Andrea and Nicolò among them, made violins and cellos.

clue.text: Cyril's dreadful poems

indicators.note: dreadful suggests something done badly, so the letters of the name are scrambled

explanation.surface: Someone called Cyril writes terrible verse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dreadful' shuffles all six letters of CYRILS, the S included.
explanation.definitionFit: Short poems, especially those written to be sung, are lyrics.

clue.text: Novelist eponymously associated with poet by Simon Raven

definitions.text: eponymously associated with poet by Simon Raven
definitions.meaning: Raven's novel ... Gray names its hero with this word beside the surname of the poet Thomas Gray

explanation.definitionFit: Henry Fielding wrote Tom Jones, and Raven's title Fielding Gray joins that name to the poet Gray's.

clue.text: Said of breakfast food regularly produced by Dickens

indicators.note: said of signals the sound of a spoken word rather than its spelling

parts.note: cereal, such as cornflakes, is a breakfast food

explanation.surface: Someone is talking about what to eat in the morning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Said of' signals that CEREAL is only heard. Dickens published most of his novels in monthly parts.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickens issued his novels in instalments, a story published in parts at regular intervals.

clue.text: His English was basic, and his criticism practical

definitions.text: His English was basic, and his criticism practical

parts.words: His English was basic, and his criticism practical
parts.note: points to the critic I.A., who co-devised Basic English and wrote Practical Criticism

explanation.definitionFit: I.A. Richards helped create Basic English with C.K. Ogden and published Practical Criticism in 1929.

clue.text: Lawrence poem, part of the Great Hebridean cycle

indicators.note: part of says the letters are a section taken from inside the following words

explanation.surface: A poem said to come from a sequence about the Hebrides.
explanation.walkthrough: 'part of' takes the letters from 'greaT HE BRIDEan'; 'cycle' only completes the scene.
explanation.definitionFit: D.H. Lawrence's poem about his mother's corpse is titled with these two words.

clue.text: Ten support Belgian province to produce Venetian senator

indicators.note: in a down clue the supporting piece goes underneath, so it follows in the answer

parts.note: Brabant is a province (now split) of Belgium
ten written as the figures 1 and 0 gives the letters I and O

explanation.surface: Ten people back a Belgian province to produce a senator from Venice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'support' in a down clue puts IO below BRABANT; 'to produce' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: In Othello, Desdemona's father is the Venetian senator Brabantio.

clue.text: Psalm found on church stool 51

parts.note: Psalm 51 begins with the Latin for 'have mercy', and the same word names a hinged choir-stall seat

explanation.definitionFit: Psalm 51 opens with this Latin plea for mercy, and a misericord ledge in church stalls is also called by it.

clue.text: Poet's party

parts.note: points to the play The ... Party by the poet T.S. Eliot

explanation.definitionFit: T.S. Eliot's verse drama is The Cocktail Party, so the poet's party is a mixed-drinks gathering.

clue.text: Constructor (from Thrace) of Alexander's Bridge

indicators.note: from here signals that the letters are reworked out of the word that follows

explanation.surface: The builder of a bridge for Alexander came from Thrace, as he might have done.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' rearranges THRACE. Alexander's Bridge was Willa Cather's first novel, so its constructor is its author.
explanation.definitionFit: Willa Cather wrote Alexander's Bridge (1912), about a bridge engineer, so she built the book.

clue.text: Those of Babylon are found in Arden

definitions.text: Those of Babylon are found in Arden

parts.words: Those of Babylon are found in Arden
parts.note: John Arden wrote a play titled after the psalm line 'by the rivers of Babylon'

explanation.walkthrough: Arden looks like Shakespeare's forest, but it is the playwright John Arden, author of The Waters of Babylon (1957).
explanation.definitionFit: Psalm 137's rivers of Babylon give John Arden his play title, The Waters of Babylon.

clue.text: "The swarthy —, with wares from Spain and Afric" (Bulwer- Lytton, Harold)

definitions.text: "The swarthy —, with wares from Spain and Afric" (Bulwer- Lytton, Harold)

parts.words: "The swarthy —, with wares from Spain and Afric" (Bulwer- Lytton, Harold)
parts.note: asks for the missing word in a line from Bulwer-Lytton's novel Harold, a Moorish trader

explanation.definitionFit: A medieval Moor or Muslim Arab trading from Spain and Africa fits the gap in Bulwer-Lytton's line.

clue.text: Conveyance of New York island arranged by Dos Passos

definitions.meaning: a moving of something, or of property, from one place or owner to another

definitions.text: of New York island arranged by Dos Passos
definitions.meaning: John Dos Passos's novel Manhattan ... names the New York island and adds this word

explanation.definitionFit: Conveyance is a legal handover, and Dos Passos's 1925 novel is Manhattan Transfer.

clue.text: Part of character in Moliere's The Miser, if analysed

indicators.note: in says the letters lie inside the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: Analysing a role in Molière's comedy L'Avare.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters sit in 'miSER, IF'. 'character' means a printed letter, not a role in a play; 'analysed' only completes the scene.
explanation.definitionFit: A serif is the small stroke finishing a line of a printed letter.

clue.text: Blake thought that the strongest poison came from his laurel crown

definitions.text: Blake thought that the strongest poison came from his laurel crown

parts.words: Blake thought that the strongest poison came from his laurel crown
parts.note: quotes William Blake's couplet that the strongest poison ever known came from a Roman ruler's laurel crown

explanation.definitionFit: Blake's Auguries of Innocence says the strongest poison came from the laurel of the Roman dictator.

clue.text: Reported which town?

parts.note: spoken, 'which town' sounds like 'witch town', the Massachusetts town of the 1692 trials

explanation.walkthrough: Heard, 'which' is 'witch': the town is the one famous for its witch trials.
explanation.definitionFit: The Massachusetts town held the notorious 1692 witch trials, so it is the witch town.

clue.text: Bennett gave him his share (he had his pride, no doubt)

definitions.text: Bennett gave him his share (he had his pride, no doubt)

parts.words: Bennett gave him his share (he had his pride, no doubt)
parts.note: Arnold Bennett's novel The ... Share names the beast whose family group is called a pride

explanation.definitionFit: Arnold Bennett wrote The Lion's Share, and a group of the big cats is a pride.

clue.text: Ivy Compton-Burnett implied he should be better

definitions.text: Ivy Compton-Burnett implied he should be better

parts.words: Ivy Compton-Burnett implied he should be better
parts.note: the novel title ... and Betters, by Ivy Compton-Burnett, pairs older people with superiors

explanation.definitionFit: Compton-Burnett's novel Elders and Betters joins the senior person to his betters.

clue.text: Form mastered by Richardson: his characters corresponded so well

definitions.text: Form mastered by Richardson: his characters corresponded so well

parts.words: Form mastered by Richardson: his characters corresponded so well
parts.note: Samuel Richardson wrote Pamela and Clarissa as exchanges of letters between characters

explanation.definitionFit: Richardson's novels are told in letters, the letter-writing form of fiction.

clue.text: Powell characters not found in the morning room

definitions.text: Powell characters not found in the morning room

parts.words: Powell characters not found in the morning room
parts.note: Anthony Powell's second novel is named for idle people of the later part of the day, not the morning

explanation.definitionFit: Anthony Powell's 1931 novel takes its title from people who belong to the time after midday.
